markers.title: The shift is the context, so nothing later has to ask for it
markers.finding: The blueprint records that a team member rarely uses the QR code directly because it needs a phone, may use a shared tablet in the office if there is one, and during a rush makes a mental note for later.
markers.decision: Restaurant, shift, station and the manager on duty sit in the header. Everything the report needs about where and when is already answered before the person taps anything.
markers.rejected: A site and shift picker inside the form, which asks a casual team member for details the roster already holds.

markers.title: One action, and it promises the thing that was missing
markers.finding: The barrier was not fear. Team members trusted their managers and nobody described feeling embarrassed to report. The barrier was the form, the phone and the threshold.
markers.decision: A single action fills the width at the top of the screen, sized for one thumb, and its second line answers both live objections: it takes under a minute, and you will hear back.
markers.rejected: A grid of entry tiles for incident, hazard, near miss and chemical spill, which makes the person classify before they have described anything.

markers.title: The loop is the first thing on the screen, not a notification
markers.finding: 18 of the 41 survey respondents who answered the question said they never or rarely learn the outcome of a report, and restaurant visits confirmed that most team members never hear what happened.
markers.decision: This person's own outcomes sit directly under the action, each naming the fix, the day they reported it and who did it. Reporting again starts from evidence that the last one worked.
markers.rejected: A push notification at the moment of closing, which arrives when the person is off shift and is gone by the time they next open the app.
markers.pattern: Hers, home with a request in review — https://mobbin.com/screens/e36b5e4e-8334-43c8-a1a4-4f71ea9f8043

markers.title: The restaurant's count, not a personal score
markers.finding: The safety team's view was that an incentive on hazard reports gets you reports, not fewer hazards, and the field evidence agreed. The proposal recognises outcomes rather than volume.
markers.decision: The number on the team member's screen counts things fixed at this restaurant, with how many started as a team report. It rewards the outcome and belongs to everyone.
markers.rejected: A personal reports-submitted count with a streak, which is exactly the incentive the research rejected.

markers.title: The threshold question, answered before the shift
markers.finding: Team members said they had never been told the threshold, so each person sets their own. Is a small cut reportable? A near miss?
markers.decision: The two articles that resolve the threshold sit on the home screen with a read time, so the question is answered before the moment it blocks someone rather than during it.
markers.rejected: A policy link in a settings menu, which nobody opens on shift.

markers.title: Three destinations, because there are only three things to do
markers.finding: The platform was configured for one workflow and used through another, and the research found that a team member's whole relationship with it is reporting something and finding out what happened.
markers.decision: Home, my reports and me. No module list, no dashboard, nothing the manager's side needs. The team member's app is a different product from the manager's, on the same system.
markers.rejected: The manager's navigation shrunk to phone size, which is how the reporting platform came to be used through managers in the first place.
